title: Query keys: the cache's identity
objectives: Explain why the query key — not the `queryFn` — decides which cache entry a `useQuery` call reads, fetches and shares
Diagnose a key that misses a `queryFn` input from its symptoms: a filter change that never fetches, or two components sharing one entry
Predict whether two keys are the same entry: object property order and `undefined` properties don't count; array order, `5` vs `"5"` and per-render values do
Write a key factory ordered general → specific, and predict which cached keys a prefix such as `todoKeys.lists()` matches

sources.title: TanStack Query v5 docs: Query Keys

questions.prompt: `<OpenTodos />` calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: () => fetchTodos('open') })` and `<DoneTodos />` calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: () => fetchTodos('done') })`. Both mount on the same page. What happens?

options.text: One request; both components show the same list — the one fetched by whichever mounted first
Two requests; each component shows its own filter, because each has its own `queryFn`
Two requests; both components show whichever response arrives last
TanStack Query throws, because two different functions are registered for one key

questions.explanation: The key is the cache entry; the `queryFn` only says how to fill it. Same key → same entry, and the second component joins the fetch already in flight (fetches are deduped by key), so its function doesn't run. Nothing throws: the library has no way to know the two functions fetch different things — that's what the key is for. Two requests would need two keys: `['todos', { status }]`.

questions.prompt: Clicking the **Done** tab updates `status` and the tab highlight, but the list still shows open todos and no request appears in the network tab. The query is `useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos', 'list'], queryFn: () => fetchTodos(status) })`. What's going on?

options.text: `status` isn't in the key, so the hook stays on the same entry and nothing triggers a fetch
The `queryFn` closure is stale: it still captures `open` from the first render's scope
`staleTime` is too long; with `staleTime: 0` a change to `status` would trigger a refetch
Nothing is wrong with the key; you're expected to call `refetch()` in an effect when `status` changes

questions.explanation: Fetches are triggered by events — a new entry, a mount, a window focus, an invalidation — not by the `queryFn` changing. The hook receives the new function on every render (so it isn't stale), but with an unchanged key nothing asks it to run. `staleTime` is already 0 by default, and staleness only matters once something triggers a fetch. A `refetch()` effect would fetch, but into the *same* entry: the two filters keep overwriting each other, and switching back shows the wrong list until the request lands. Put `status` in the key.

questions.prompt: Which pair of keys refers to the **same** cache entry?

options.text: `['todos', { status: 'open', page: 2 }]` and `['todos', { page: 2, status: 'open' }]`
`['todos', 'open', 2]` and `['todos', 2, 'open']`
`['todos', { status: 'open' }]` and `['todos', { status: 'open', sort: null }]`

questions.explanation: Keys are hashed from their JSON with object properties sorted, so property order inside an object never matters. Array positions do, and `5` and `"5"` serialise differently. The `null` pair is the subtle one: only `undefined` properties are dropped from the hash — `null` is a real JSON value, so `sort: null` makes a different key.

questions.prompt: `api` is a module-level HTTP client. Which values belong in the key for `queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.get('/projects', { params: { orgId, archived }, signal })`?

options.text: `orgId` and `archived`
`orgId`, `archived` and `api`
`orgId`, `archived` and `signal`
Only a label such as `'projects'` — the closure always reads the latest `orgId` and `archived`

questions.explanation: The key holds the values that identify the data and can change: `orgId` and `archived`. The client is the thing you call, not an input — the official `exhaustive-deps` lint rule says function call targets aren't key dependencies. `signal` is created by the library for each fetch and handed to the `queryFn`; it isn't yours to key on. And a label-only key brings back both bugs: different orgs share one entry, and changing `orgId` triggers no fetch.

questions.prompt: With the reading's factory (`lists: () => [...todoKeys.all, 'list']`), which cached queries does `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: todoKeys.lists() })` match? Pick all that apply.

options.text: `['todos', 'list', { status: 'open', page: 1 }]`
`['todos', 'list', { status: 'done', page: 3 }]`
`['todos', 'detail', 5, { preview: true }]`
`['todos-list', { status: 'open', page: 1 }]`
`['todos']`

questions.explanation: A filter key matches every cached key that **starts with it**, element by element. `['todos', 'list']` is the start of both list keys, whatever their filters. The detail key diverges at position 1 (`'detail'`); `'todos-list'` is one string, not `'todos'` followed by `'list'` — elements are compared whole; and `['todos']` is *shorter* than the filter — a prefix of the filter, not the other way round. That asymmetry is what lets you invalidate "every list" without touching details.

questions.prompt: Lists are keyed `['todos', 'list', filters]`, but a teammate keyed the detail `['todo', id]`. After a bulk *mark all done*, the code calls `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })`. What breaks?

options.text: An open detail stays stale: `['todo', 5]` doesn't start with `['todos']`
Nothing — `'todo'` and `'todos'` share a prefix, so the detail is matched too
The lists are missed as well, because the invalidation key doesn't include their filter objects
Every query in the app is invalidated, because a one-element key matches everything

questions.explanation: Matching compares whole elements: `'todo'` and `'todos'` are different strings, full stop. The lists *are* matched, because a shorter filter matches any key that starts with it — you never need the filters to reach every variant. And `['todos']` only matches keys whose first element is `'todos'`. Root every key of a feature at one `all` key, and this class of miss disappears.

questions.prompt: The list primes the detail cache with `setQueryData(todoKeys.detail(todo.id), todo)`, where `todo.id` is `5`. The detail route builds its key by hand as `['todos', 'detail', params.id]`, with `params.id` read from the URL. What does the user see when they open todo 5?

options.text: A loading state and a fresh request: `'5'` and `5` are different keys
The primed todo instantly — keys are compared loosely, like `==`
The primed todo instantly, then a background refetch because primed data is stale
An error, because TanStack Query rejects string ids in keys

questions.explanation: The hash is the key's JSON, and `5` and `"5"` serialise differently, so these are two entries. The primed data sits unused, the detail page fetches, and a later `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: todoKeys.detail(5) })` misses the string-keyed entry too. Option three is what you'd get if the keys *matched* (the default `staleTime: 0` makes primed data stale at once). Strings are perfectly legal in keys — they just have to be the same strings. Normalise with `Number(params.id)` and go through the factory.

prompts.prompt: Complete the factory: each list is keyed by its filters, and each detail sits under the feature's root.
prompts.explanation: Every key starts from `todoKeys.all`, so `['todos']` reaches the whole feature; `lists()` and `details()` are the branches you'll invalidate; and the last element carries the `queryFn`'s inputs — the filter object for a list, the id for a detail.

prompts.prompt: Make the `queryFn` take its filters *from the key* (built by the factory as `['todos', 'list', filters]`), so it can't read an input the key doesn't hold.
prompts.explanation: The `queryFn` receives a context object — `queryKey`, `signal`, `client`, `meta` — and the key it gets is the one the entry is filed under. Reading the filters from position 2 instead of from the surrounding scope means there is no outside variable left to forget: whatever the function fetches, the key already identifies. With an `as const` factory, `queryKey[2]` is even typed as the filters.

prompts.prompt: Invalidate only the bare `['todos']` entry — not every key that starts with it.
prompts.explanation: Filters match by prefix unless you pass `exact: true`, which turns the key into an exact match. Without it, `['todos']` would reach every list and detail under the root.

prompts.prompt: Define the key and its function together, so no component can pair a key with the wrong function.
prompts.explanation: `queryOptions` returns its argument unchanged at runtime; its value is in TypeScript, where the key is tagged with the data type. `queryClient.getQueryData(todoDetail(5).queryKey)` is then typed as the todo, which a hand-written key can't give you.

code: const fetchTodos = (status: string) => { requests.push(status); return api.todos(status); };
const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["todos"], queryFn: () => fetchTodos("open") });
const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["todos"], queryFn: () => fetchTodos("done") });
// <OpenTodos /> then <DoneTodos /> mount together on a fresh QueryClient.
// The server has one open todo ("Buy milk") and one done todo ("File taxes").
snippets.question: Once the data arrives, what do the two paragraphs say, and what's in `requests`?
snippets.answer: "Open: Buy milk" and "Done: Buy milk"; requests is ["open"]
acceptable: both show Buy milk, one request (open)
Open: Buy milk / Done: Buy milk, ["open"]
snippets.explanation: One key, one entry. `OpenTodos` mounts first and starts the fetch; `DoneTodos` mounts while it's in flight and joins it instead of fetching again, so `fetchTodos("done")` doesn't run. When the response lands, both components render the same entry. This was run headlessly against v5.104: one request, both paragraphs "Buy milk".

code: const a = hashKey(["todos", { status: "open", page: 1, sort: undefined }]);
snippets.question: What's logged?
snippets.explanation: `hashKey` is the function the cache uses: `JSON.stringify` with plain objects' keys sorted. So `a` and `b` match — order doesn't count and the `undefined` property is dropped. The surprise is `c === d`: a `Set` (like a `Map`) isn't a plain object and JSON has no form for it, so both serialise as `{}` and every Set-valued key collides. Pass `[...tags].sort()` instead.

code: queryFn: () => fetchFeed(since), // the server answers in about 20 ms
// Feed mounts once; nothing else happens on the page.
snippets.question: How many requests does `Feed` make?
snippets.answer: It never stops — about one request per response (44 in the first second when measured)
snippets.explanation: Each response re-renders `Feed` a few milliseconds later, the new render builds a new `since`, so a new key — a new entry with no data — and that triggers another fetch. Run headlessly with a 20 ms fake server, it made 44 requests and 44 cache entries in one second and kept going. A key holds the request's *inputs*; a clock read during render is not an input, it's a new identity per render.
